summary.text: Medieval Islamic astronomy covers the astronomical developments made in the Islamic world, especially during the Islamic Golden Age, and mostly written in Arabic.
It built on Greek, Sassanid, and Indian works that were translated and developed into a science with Islamic characteristics.
Latin translations of Arabic works in the 12th century helped revive ancient astronomy, and stars such as Aldebaran, Altair, and Deneb still carry Arabic names.

facts.label: Main period
facts.value: The Islamic Golden Age, 9th to 13th centuries

facts.label: Surviving texts
facts.value: About 10,000 manuscripts, many unread or uncatalogued

facts.label: First translations
facts.value: The first astronomical texts rendered into Arabic were Indian and Persian

items.prompt: A community must know when the five daily prayers fall and which way to face. How did that need relate to astronomy?

options.label: It pushed scholars away from the sky and toward geography
It inspired progress in astronomy
It had no link, since prayer times were fixed by custom alone
It was settled entirely by Ptolemy's Almagest

items.explain: The obligation to determine the five daily prayer times and the qibla, the direction of the Kaaba in Mecca, inspired intellectual progress in astronomy.

items.prompt: How did Arabs study the sky before Islam, unlike the Babylonians, Greeks and Indians?

options.label: With elaborate mathematical systems of their own
With tables taken from the Sasanian Empire
With the sine function copied from India
With observations of when particular stars rose and set

items.explain: The pre-Islamic Arabs relied on empirical observations of the rising and setting of particular stars, a tradition called Anwā'. Mathematics was introduced to it after Islamization.

items.prompt: An Arab astronomer drops the chords of arc used in Greek trigonometry for a tool borrowed from elsewhere. What does he adopt?

options.label: The sine function, taken from India
The equant, taken from Ptolemy
The zij, taken from the Babylonians
The analemma, taken from Persia

items.explain: Fragments of texts show that Arab astronomers adopted the sine function from India in place of the chords of arc used in Greek trigonometry.

items.prompt: Before al-Khwarizmi's Zij al-Sindhind in 830, Islamic astronomers mostly translated foreign works. What did his work mark?

options.label: The end of astronomy in Baghdad
A return to the earlier star-rising tradition
A turning point, when they began to develop new ideas
The first translation of the Almagest into Arabic

items.explain: It was the first major Muslim work of astronomy and introduced Ptolemaic concepts. It marked a turning point from translating works to developing new ideas.

items.prompt: Ibn al-Haytham wrote a book called "Doubts on Ptolemy". Did it reject Earth sitting at the centre of the universe?

options.label: Yes, it replaced the idea with a Sun-centred model
Yes, it proved the Earth moves through space
No, it criticised parts of Ptolemy's theories without disputing that model
No, it defended every part of Ptolemy's work

items.explain: Ibn al-Haytham did not dispute the geocentric model but criticised elements of Ptolemy's theories, and other astronomers went on to develop alternate models that resolved the problems he found.

items.prompt: A European scholar in the 1100s wants to recover ancient astronomy that was lost in the early medieval period. Where could he find it?

options.label: In Greek originals kept safely in every cathedral library
In Latin translations of Arabic works
In books newly written by Babylonian astronomers
In the oral lore of Roman farmers

items.explain: Islamic astronomy played a significant role in reviving ancient astronomy after the loss of knowledge in the early medieval period, notably through Latin translations of Arabic works in the 12th century.
